3313.prule: No distinctive stress (loudness). Every root carries a lexically arbitrary long or short penultimate vowel (the Central Philippine accent contrast) with minimal pairs (salug 'floor' vs sa:lug 'river'); length is confined to a non-final vowel before a single consonant, is non-distinctive on the final vowel, never precedes a consonant cluster in inherited words, and shifts to the root-final vowel or is imposed on the penult under affixation. Accent placement is therefore listed per root, not computable from syllable count or weight.
3313.srule: Not mentioned in McFarland 1974, Ch. 2 (pp. 29-42); his only stress statement is that 'stress, or loudness, is not' distinctive (p. 31), with the contrast carried by lexical penult vowel length.

3314.dq: there is a phonological clause stress which contrasts with phonological word stress. ... That is, a clause-final high tone syllable receives a strong stress only if it is the only high-tone syllable in the word. Otherwise it is unstressed. In cases where the final syllable of the clause is not marked by high tone, the rules for phonological word apply.
3314.heavy: Not a weight system; but within the tone-driven rules a final CLOSED high-tone syllable (type 3 CVQ, closed by glottal stop) gets light stress while other final high-tone syllables are unstressed, and the L-H penult rule applies only 'if the final syllable is an open one' (pp. 154-155).
3314.prule: Stress is not positional: every syllable carries one of two register tones (H/L) and word stress is assigned from the tone pattern by an ordered rule set with four degrees. Heavy stress on a H syllable followed by a L syllable; medium stress on the first of a run of H syllables; light stress on a final closed (glottal-stop-final) H syllable, other final H syllables unstressed; in words ending L-H with an open final syllable, light stress on the penult; L syllables otherwise unstressed. A word may carry more than one stress.
3314.srule: Tone-conditioned, graded, non-rhythmic: a word is 'marked by one or more stresses' with four degrees (heavy, medium, light, unstressed). Besides heavy stress on a H syllable before a L syllable: medium stress on the first of a series of H syllables; light stress on a word-final closed (glottal-final) H syllable, other final H syllables unstressed; light stress on the low-tone penult of a word ending L-H when the final syllable is open; L syllables otherwise unstressed. No alternating secondary stress is described.
3314.quote: A phonological word is a phonological unit consisting of one or more phonological syllables and marked by one or more stresses which are predictable from the tone pattern of the word. A high tone receives heavy stress if followed by a low-tone syllable ... The first in a series of high-tone syllables within a word receives a medium stress ... A final closed high-tone syllable receives light stress ..…

3314.tone: Two phonemic register tones, one per syllable; 'There are probably not a dozen minimal tone pairs in the language... altogether tone carries a very low functional load' (p. 5); 'The type of stress within a phonological word is predictable from the tone pattern' (p. 6). Appendix B pp. 154-155 gives the six ordered tone-to-stress rules (four degrees of stress): (1) H heavy if followed by L; (2) first of a run of H syllables medium; (3) final closed H light; (4) other final H unstressed; (5) L penult light when the final is an open H; (6) L otherwise unstressed. Deibler 1992 Alekano OPD p. 3 ('There are several degrees of stress conditioned by tone... Alekano has two phonemic tones. They are not written in the practical orthography because they have an extremely low functional load.') agrees that stress is tone-conditioned but states the lesser-stress rules differently. Young 1962 pp. 98-99: Gahuku has 'a phoneme of tone', minimal pairs musi / mu'si; no separate stress rule given for Gahuku.

3315.heavy: 'The most important factor of sonority is the vowel length': syllables with a long vowel attract the stronger stress. Secondary attractors: a following/preceding sonorous consonant (y, l, nasals) and, per Bergsland 1994, 'the open- or closedness of the syllables' (unspecified). Taff 1992: 'weight is assigned at the nuclear level so that consonants are weightless. Syllables containing long vowels are heavy' (as quoted by Rozelle 1997:91).
3315.dflt: Eastern: penult (weaker stress often on the initial syllable); Atkan/Attuan: initial ('the stronger stress on the first syllable is more prevalent'); four short syllables: trochaic rhythm; a sonorous consonant may shift the stress one syllable toward it
3315.prule: Non-phonemic, weight-sensitive and partly fluctuating: the strongest stress goes to a syllable with a long vowel (in disyllables: initial unless the second vowel is long, then final; long vowels attract stress in longer forms too). Among short syllables the default is dialect-specific: Eastern (Unalaska/Pribilof/Umnak) penult if the final syllable is short, final if long; Atkan/Attuan initial. Sonorous consonants (y, l, nasals), closed syllables and phrase rhythm may pull the stress one syllable away from the default. Taff 1992 / Rozelle 1997 state the Eastern (Pribilof) rule plainly: 'Stress falls on the ultimate syllable if it is heavy and the penultimate syllable is light. Otherwise, stress falls on the penultimate syllable' (long vowels heavy, consonants weightless).
3315.srule: A weaker (delimiting) stress frequently falls on the word-initial syllable: 'the initial syllable of polysyllabic words has frequently more than weakest stress' (1997:30); Eastern: stronger stress penult/final 'and a weaker stress frequently falls on the first syllable' (1994: xx). Forms of four short syllables 'tend to have a trochaic rhythm but relatively sonorous consonants may break it' (1997:31). No placement stated for longer forms beyond long-vowel attraction and sonority effects; all statements are tendencies.
3315.quote: [p. 30] Stress is not phonemic. In so far as the initial syllable of polysyllabic words has frequently more than weakest stress, stress has a certain delimiting function. 3317.dq: En este artículo, hemos ofrecido una primera aproximación a los patrones prosódicos básicos de la palabra amahuaca. La palabra amahuaca exhibe, de manera simultánea, un rasgo de tono léxico y una estructura métrica basada en la formación de pies trocaicos de izquierda a derecha. [p. 104]

3317.prule: Tone language: a single lexical high tone (H vs. Ø, no L or M); every word carries at least one H and never two adjacent H; the position of H in a morphologically simple word is unpredictable (11 patterns over 6 syllable shapes); no primary word stress can be posited (culminativity unmet), so the authors do not call the word's metrical structure stress.
3317.srule: No secondary stress as such: the source posits no primary stress and calls the word's rhythm 'estructura métrica', not 'acento (stress)'. Rhythmic (metrical) prominence: trochaic feet built left to right, (σ́σ)(σ́σ)…, so odd-numbered syllables are foot heads and even-numbered syllables are weak (nasal codas survive only in odd syllables; in complex words H tone is shifted off even syllables onto the next head); degenerate final feet allowed; all heads of equal rank, none primary (culminativity unmet).

tn.translation: Consequently, we can analyse the tone contrasts in Amahuaca in two ways: H vs. L or H vs. Ø. 3321.dq: For both Balti and Rebkong Amdo, stress falls on the second syllable (σ2) of disyllabic non-verbs — nouns, adjectives, and numerals.
3321.dloc: Caplow 2016 LTBA 39(2): author's abstract, p. 180, on the open publisher page (jbe-platform.com); body pp. 180-221 paywalled, not opened. Supporting: Caplow 2016 HL 15(2) abstract p. 1 and fn. 3 p. 2; Tournadre & Suzuki 2023 sec. 7.3.3 pp. 241-242; Lim 2018 sec. 1.3.3.1 pp. 24-25.
3321.prule: Stress position is set by lexical category (word class), not by syllable count or weight: disyllabic non-verbs (nouns, adjectives, numerals) are stressed on the second syllable (σ2); disyllabic verbs are never stressed on σ2 and, on limited Rebkong Amdo data, are stressed on the first syllable (σ1), the pattern Caplow documents in full for Balti (HL 15(2) abstract: 'Verbs, in contrast, are stressed on the first syllable (σ1)... distinguishing stress patterns by lexical category'). Only disyllables are described for Amdo; stress is non-contrastive, cued mainly by higher pitch (Caplow 2009: 527-528 per Lim 2018: 23-24, opened). No weight condition is mentioned for Amdo.
3321.srule: Not mentioned in Caplow 2016 (LTBA 39(2)), abstract p. 180 — the only part of the primary source that could be opened (body pp. 181-221 paywalled); the abstract describes disyllables only. Nothing on Amdo secondary stress in Caplow 2016 HL 15(2) (fn. 3), Suzuki 2017: 42-43, Tribur 2020: 67, Tournadre & Suzuki 2023: 241, 529, or Ebihara 2024: 6.
3321.quote: This paper offers a synchronic description of stress patterns in two conservative varieties of Tibetan, and a diachronic reconstruction of stress patterns in Proto-Tibetan. For both Balti and Rebkong Amdo, stress falls on the second syllable (σ2) of disyllabic non-verbs — nouns, adjectives, and numerals. ... Disyllabic verbs are never stressed on σ2. For Balti, robust evidence shows that they are stressed on the first syllable (σ1). Limited data for Rebkong Amdo suggests the same pattern. Thus σ1 stress is tentatively reconstructed for verbs in Proto-Tibetan.
3321.loc: Caplow 2016 LTBA 39(2): author's abstract, p. 180, on the open publisher page (jbe-platform.com); body pp. 180-221 paywalled, not opened. Supporting: Caplow 2016 HL 15(2) abstract p. 1 and fn. 3 p. 2; Tournadre & Suzuki 2023 sec. 7.3.3 pp. 241-242; Lim 2018 sec. 1.3.3.1 pp. 24-25.

3321.exq_: Disyllabic verbs are never stressed on σ2. For Balti, robust evidence shows that they are stressed on the first syllable (σ1). Limited data for Rebkong Amdo suggests the same pattern. [Under the two-class rule the verb branch is part of the rule, not an exception; the abstract names no exceptions t…
3321.tone: Amdo Tibetan is non-tonal in every opened source: Makley et al. 1999: 112 ('nor are there tonal distinctions', Labrang); Ebihara 2010: 43 ('Amdo Tibetan has no tonal opposition'); Suzuki 2017 SAG7 Table 1 (Northeastern/Amdo distinctive suprasegmentals n/a) and p. 42 ('dialects of Amdo are likely to possess a suprasegmental distinction by stress... it may be distinctive or rather a prosodic feature'); Tournadre & Suzuki 2023 sec. 9.5.6 ('does not have distinctive suprasegmental features. However, the position of stress may affect some phonetic realisations'; Gorkä Amdo reported tonal). Ebihara 2024: 6 (Gonghe nomad dialect): non-distinctive word pitch patterns 'like Japanese accent', e.g. first syllable low, second and later syllables high — consistent with σ2 prominence.

3326.dq: Nembi has two basic sentence types: verbal and non-verbal. Sentence-final intonation, a rapid decline in pitch, is superimposed on the final word of all sentences. (Chapter 5 'Sentences', 'Basic sentence types', printed p. 49; the only other prosodic statements are sentence/paragraph-level intonation and pitch, printed pp. 18 and 22, none about word stress)
3326.prule: No word-stress rule is stated anywhere in the source. The only word-level prosodic statement is that Nembi has two phonemic tones (high vs. low), with low functional load, exemplified by the tonal contrast between otherwise identical second-person (low) and third-person (high) verb endings; tone is not written in the texts.
3326.quote: Nembi has two phonemic tones: high and low. In the verb charts, second and third person forms which appear to be identical are distinguished by tone. Second person endings have low tone, and third person endings have high. Tone, however, carries a low functional load in the language and is not written. In discourse, the context makes second and third person referents clear, and tone is not marked.
3326.loc: Appendix B 'Final verb affixation for person number tense and mode', p. 79 (heading on p. 78)
3326.idn: Nembi (Franklin's Magi; Angal Heneng South / angal enen); no sub-dialect named; data: Nembi Valley and Nembi Plateau, Southern Highlands Province, Papua New Guinea; author's fieldwork 1970-1979 under the auspices of Christian Union Mission; corpus of fourteen texts (four procedural, ten narrative)
3326.tone: Two phonemic tones, high and low; low functional load; not written in the orthography and not marked in the texts; the illustrated contrast is morphological (2nd-person verb endings low, 3rd-person high). The source never uses the words stress or accent for Nembi (its single 'stress' token, p. 9, is Halliday on English theme), so it neither asserts nor denies word stress; the reading tone or pitch accent rests on the tone statement plus the absence of any stress rule, and a reviewer preferring not determinable from the sources for a four-sentence tone note in a discourse study would not be contradicting the text.

3328.dloc: Litteral 2008 [1980]: Chapter III 'A Sketch of Angor Phonology and Grammar', section 'Foot', pp. 23-24. Litteral 1997 OPD: p. 4, section 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)'.
3328.prule: Primary stress is lexically contrastive (phonemic) and falls on one of the last three syllables of the phonological word (ultima, penult or antepenult), with no rule given for which; the source marks it lexically ('Phonemic stress is indicated by ′'). Post-nuclear syllables are unstressed; foot-final i is never stressed. OPD: 'Stress is phonemic.' with minimal pairs a'ri 'tree sp.' / 'arɨ 'string bag'; a'mboko 'beetle' / ama'ro 'she sits'; mana'ŋgo 'she stands' / ma'naŋgo 'mushroom sp.'.
3328.srule: Predictable from the primary: every alternate syllable preceding the primary (nucleus) has secondary stress, counted leftward from the primary (the syllable next to the primary is unstressed, the second syllable before it has secondary stress, and so on); when the syllable due for secondary stress has i or ü as its nucleus, the secondary stress falls on the preceding (next leftward) syllable instead. Examples asifú = à.si.fú; hoemariheyándi = hwemàriheyándi. Syllables after the primary are unstressed.
3328.quote: The Angor foot, or phonological word, is the phonological unit above the syllable in the phonological hierarchy. It is the domain within which stress rules operate. There are three phonetic degrees of stress but only the nucleus of the foot needs to be indicated as the degree of stress on other syllables can be predicted on the basis of stress rules. 3330.dq: Koch 2014 p.320: "in Arandic language stress is usually on the first syllable with an onset, which usually means the second syllable of the word"; Breen 2001 p.53: "it conditions primary stress and perhaps additional length on the initial vowel of the word"; Breen's p.63 examples are citation-form words.
3330.dloc: Koch 2014 p. 320; Breen 2001 p. 53 (sec. 3.1) and p. 63 (sec. 4.7, items (b), (d)).
3330.heavy: Not rime weight. The conditioning factor is the presence of a consonant onset: 'the first vowel that follows a consonant' (Breen p.55), 'the first syllable with an onset' (Koch 2014 p.320), 'the first syllable beginning with a consonant (i.e. (V)'CV)' (Koch 1997 p.285). An onsetless word-initial vowel is skipped.
3330.dflt: Not applicable in rime terms: every word contains a consonant, so the first onsetful syllable is always the first or second; an onsetless initial syllable is skipped and stress falls on the second syllable (Breen: uniformly the second VC(C) syllable).
3330.prule: Main stress on the first vowel that follows a consonant, i.e. on the first syllable that has a consonant onset: the second syllable in vowel-initial words (the majority), the first in consonant-initial words. Under Breen's VC(C) syllabification (all Arandic words underlyingly vowel-initial, initial /e/ silent utterance-initially) this is uniformly the second underlying syllable, which would be the grid 01 010 0100 01000 010000 0100000 01000000 in underlying syllables.
3330.srule: Not mentioned in Breen 2001 (secs 3-4.7, pp. 51-64 read; no secondary-stress rule for Anmatyerr or Arandic). His Western Anmatyerr transcriptions (pp. 62-63) mark one stress per word, including four-syllable [atántətʲɛː] atanthetyeh; the only grave (secondary) accent is on the second member of the reduplication [ɭkɛ́rəmbɪɭkɛ̀r] rlkerremperlkerr (p. 62).

3334.heavy: Not weight: Delafosse says the accent 'est indépendant de l'allongement ou de la brièveté de certaines voyelles'; the conditioning he states is vowel quality (a, o attract the accent; e, u, i repel it).
3334.prule: Two-tone language (H, L; contours HL, LH; downstep) per all Morofo-specific modern descriptions (Koffi 2009, 2014, 2018, 2021, 2022), none of which states a word-stress position. The only positional accent statement is Delafosse 1900 (language-level Anyi, pre-tonological): default penult; final if final vowel is a or o unless the penult also has a/o; in 3+-syllable words with penult e/u/i, antepenult unless final a/o claims it (a preferred over o); prefix a- never accented and not counted; monosyllables unaccented unless emphasised.
3334.srule: Not described within simple words (Delafosse 1900 §I 'Accent', pp.115-117: one accented syllable per word, monosyllables unaccented; Koffi 2009-2022 silent). Only in compounds: in compounds of two nouns, two verbs, or noun+verb each component keeps its accent in its own place (Delafosse rule 6).

There are two contour tones: High-Low and Low-High' (2009:19); 'L'agni est une langue tonale' (2018 §8.0); tone contrastive lexically and grammatically with downstep/downdrift (2014:179-180) but very low functional load (~74 tonal minimal pairs in 4,539 words, RFL 1.63%, Koffi 2022). Koffi 2022:66-67 translates Delafosse's passage with 'tone'/'pitch'/'stress' interchangeably, says he 'vacillates between terms such as tone, pitch, stress, and musical intonation', and endorses him: 'All in all, Delafosse's insights about Anyi are accurate, and so is his characterization of the Anyi prosodic system'; Koffi argues Anyi straddles tone / pitch-accent / accent typologies (F0, intensity and duration all cue grammatical moods) but gives no syllable position for stress.

3338.dq: Primary stress in the default case falls on the penultimate syllable of the prosodic word, but more sonorous vowels also tend to attract stress. (Parker 2009 p.6; the OPD p.7 states its rule under 'General rules for stress' at word level with no phrase-level discussion)
3338.dloc: Parker 2009: sec. 2 'Data' (2.1 'Basic facts'), p.6, paragraph after example set (3); Boevé & Boevé 2005 OPD: p.7, 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)'.
3338.heavy: Not syllable quantity: the stress-attracting property is vowel sonority. OPD p.7 hierarchy, most to least sonorous: [a] á, [æ] é > [ɛ] e, [ʌ] a, [ɔ] o, [ø] ó > [y] ú, [u] u > [i] i > [ə̆] è, [ɜ̆] à; 'The more sonorant vowels tend to sound longer.' Parker p.6: 'more sonorous vowels also tend to attract stress.' No CVV/CVC weight mentioned; the lowest grade (è, à) are the short/reduced vowels, so a reviewer could read the bottom split as full-vs-reduced vowel weight, but the scale as stated is five-grade vowel quality.
3338.dflt: penultimate syllable of the prosodic word (Parker p.6 'in the default case'; OPD 'may be preferred on the penultimate syllable')
3338.prule: Primary stress falls by default on the penultimate syllable of the prosodic word, but the syllable whose vowel is highest on a five-grade vowel-sonority scale (á, é > e, a, o, ó > ú, u > i > è, à) attracts stress away from the penult; both sources state the sonority override as a tendency ('tend to attract', 'may be conditioned'). Conditioning is vowel quality (sonority/height), not CVV/CVC syllable quantity.
3338.srule: Secondary stress exists but its placement is not given: Parker 2009 (p.6) says /ð/ occurs 'in syllables bearing primary stress, secondary stress, or no stress at all' and marks no stress in his transcriptions; Boevé & Boevé 2005 OPD (p.7) does not mention secondary stress.
3338.quote: [Parker 2009, p.6] All syllables must contain an onset except word-initially. Primary stress in the default case falls on the penultimate syllable of the prosodic word, but more sonorous vowels also tend to attract stress.
